why_it_matters: Every attitude field (JobSatisfaction, EnvironmentSatisfaction, JobInvolvement, RelationshipSatisfaction, WorkLifeBalance) is a single 1-4 item with no published wording and unknown reliability, and in this synthetic (fictional) file the values are generated; meta-analytic estimates from multi-item scales set expectations only and do not validate any IBM field.
Younger workers have fewer side bets and more options, and age correlates negatively with voluntary turnover (rho = -.21).
Frequent travel takes time and energy from non-work roles, a recognised source of work-family conflict; no verified turnover meta-analysis exists for travel itself.
Undocumented and not interpretable as pay; exclude from substantive interpretation (MonthlyIncome is the pay variable).
Departments differ in occupation and outside labour-market options, which shape the ease of leaving.

construct: Weak proxy for commute (units undocumented; distance is not travel time)
why_it_matters: Long commutes add strain and weaken community ties; the supporting study measured travel minutes (district exit only at 40+ minutes), so this field is a weak proxy.
Education mainly affects turnover via outside options; its meta-analytic link to turnover is near zero (rho = .04, CI includes 0).

construct: Occupational labour market / ease of movement
why_it_matters: Fields differ in demand for their skills, which changes how easy it is to find another job.

construct: Facet satisfaction with the work environment (referent undocumented); single 1-4 item
why_it_matters: A poor environment is expected to lower attitudes and perceived support; this item is not a climate measure, so climate meta-analytic estimates do not validate it.
Meta-analyses find essentially no sex difference in turnover (rho = .00), so any effect needs a contextual explanation.
key_source: Rubenstein et al. 2018; Griffeth et al. 2000

why_it_matters: Undocumented and not interpretable as pay; exclude from substantive interpretation.
In the literature people who identify with their job have more to lose by leaving it; this single undocumented item only labels the construct.
Level bundles pay, seniority and promotion prospects, so its effect is confounded with income and experience.
key_source: Ference et al. 1977; Yang et al. 2019

construct: Occupation; job characteristics; ease of movement
why_it_matters: Roles differ in job design, outside demand and career paths, all of which shape the desirability and ease of leaving.

construct: Job satisfaction (desirability of movement); single 1-4 item
why_it_matters: In the literature dissatisfaction starts the withdrawal chain toward quitting; this single undocumented item only labels the construct, and links to turnover can differ by scale length (single vs multi-item).
key_source: Mobley 1977; Tett & Meyer 1993; Rubenstein et al. 2018

why_it_matters: Marriage adds community links and raises the cost of relocating; married employees quit slightly less (rho = -.10).
key_source: Mitchell et al. 2001; Rubenstein et al. 2018

construct: Pay level, confounded with job level and career stage
why_it_matters: Pay is the core inducement to stay (pay rho = -.17 in the literature), but here JobLevel explains most of income variance and 95% of the under-$2,475 group is JobLevel 1, so only within-level variation is pay as distinct from career stage.
key_source: Rubenstein et al. 2018; March & Simon 1958; Adams 1965

why_it_matters: Undocumented and not interpretable as pay; exclude from substantive interpretation.

construct: Prior job mobility (hobo syndrome; search skill)
why_it_matters: Past job changes predict future quitting, through disposition and practised job search.

construct: Job demand / workload proxy (yes/no flag; no hours, premium, or voluntariness)
why_it_matters: A binary proxy for workload demands; in Podsakoff et al.'s framework workload is a challenge stressor linked to lower turnover, and meta-analytic workload-turnover links are weak (rho = -.10), so do not label it a hindrance.
key_source: Rubenstein et al. 2018; Podsakoff et al. 2007

construct: Single-year raise percentage (at most a weak proxy for salary growth)
why_it_matters: Low salary growth is linked to exits, especially among high performers, but one year's raise percent is at most a weak proxy for salary growth.
Low and high performers can both leave more than average performers; the IBM rating takes only values 3 and 4.
Good relationships are embeddedness links in the literature, but the item does not say whom it refers to, so do not read it as LMX or as a validated peer-relations measure.
Could be read as a side bet given up by leaving, but the 0-3 coding and any vesting are undocumented, so that reading cannot be tested here.
Experience tracks age, pay and level, so it mainly indexes career stage rather than a separate driver.
Training signals investment and lowers turnover as a reward, but transferable skills can raise exits unless followed by advancement.
key_source: Benson et al. 2004; Rubenstein et al. 2018

construct: Work-life balance; related to (roughly the inverse of) work-family conflict; single 1-4 item
why_it_matters: Role conflict lowers satisfaction in the literature; balance is related to conflict but is not simply its mirror image.
Tenure builds links, fit and sacrifice and filters out poor fits; tenure rho = -.20 (-.27 excluding an outlier).
key_source: Mitchell et al. 2001; Rubenstein et al. 2018

why_it_matters: Long time in one role can mean a stalled career, which lowers attachment via perceived lack of support.
Fewer promotional chances relate to more leaving (r1 = -.12), but promotions can also raise market value and exits.
key_source: Griffeth et al. 2000; Trevor et al. 1997

construct: Duration of manager relationship (not LMX quality)
why_it_matters: Relationship length is only a proxy for LMX/supervisor support, which relates to intentions more clearly than to actual exits.
